text: From High Bridge the trail passes Howard Lake, climbs a long, hot, dusty switchback up an open southwestern shoulder, then drops into subalpine fir/pine forest and crosses a clear creek before reaching the lower of two glacial cirques on a rocky, sandy moraine. Heaton Camp (~6,700 ft), the only established camp, sits just above the terminal moraine. Another set of switchbacks above camp ends in about a third of a mile at a rocky outcropping, where the maintained trail stops. From there a talus slope leads to the base of the summit; the scramble is 'not particularly technical' but steep, with loose footing and real exposure in places, marked by faint red paint arrows, and crosses a snowfield above the Sandalee Glacier before reaching the old fire-lookout site and the radio tower at the true summit.

text: Start at the Easy Pass/Fisher Creek Trailhead on SR-20 (marked pullout near milepost 151, about 5 miles west of Rainy Pass, elevation ~3,700 ft; room for roughly 10 cars, pit toilet, no water at the lot). Follow the Easy Pass Trail, which climbs steadily through forest and then open meadows/talus, gaining roughly 2,800 ft over about 3.6 miles to Easy Pass (~6,500 ft); budget 1.5-2 hours at a good pace. There are reliable streams along the lower trail but none right at the pass, so top off water before cresting. Do not descend into Fisher Creek: leave the trail just west of the pass, before it starts switchbacking down, and begin an uncomfortable cross-country sidehill traverse west-northwest across gullies, scree, talus, grass and blocky ground, well above the valley. Around 6,500 ft the route crosses a waterfall almost directly below Mesahchie on an easy bench - the ground above and below that bench is much harder. Beyond it, climb to the basin below Mesahchie Col, a common high camp with water. From the basin, work up the crest of the shoulder between Mesahchie and Katsuk (some class 4 moves getting established) to gentler but loose, cairned terrain, then traverse slabs down to the col at the foot of Mesahchie, which has a good bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the base of the first obvious gully leading up the southwest/west ridge - steep class 3/4 at its bottom, then broadening and easing after a string of cairns - and follow it to the ridge crest, then the exposed but moderate ridgecrest to the summit. The whole approach beyond Easy Pass is loose and unmarked, so GPS or a photo of the route is worth having. Total one-way distance/gain to the summit run around 12 km and 4,900 ft of the route's overall 24.1 km / 7,480 ft round trip.

text: The climbing starts at Mesahchie Col, the col at the foot of Mesahchie's west ridge. From the basin, the shoulder crest leads up to cairned ground; follow the cairns to the base of the small peak between Mesahchie and Katsuk, turn right, and traverse slightly exposed slabs down to the col, which holds a well-built bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the first obvious gully leading up the west ridge. The right gully is steep Class 3/4 at its base, then enters a broader, gentler gully past a string of cairns and tops out on the ridge crest; the crest is then followed east, exposed but moderate, to the summit. Negative marker: if you reached the peak along the crest from the east and are starting from a flat spot at the foot of the summit pyramid, you are on the East Ridge, not this route.

text: Start at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FR-4065). Follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (Trail #707) north; the first mile crosses two significant creeks with no bridges (a log crossing, a root crossing, and one more insistent ford), so expect wet feet and use caution in early season high water. The trail then climbs steadily through forest and, after roughly 2.5 miles and about 1,950 ft of gain, reaches the last major switchback (~4,300 ft) just before the tread begins zig-zagging steeply up toward Headlee Pass. Leave the maintained trail here and traverse northeast on a surprisingly easy, cairned line across a talus field toward the Mile High buttress (the striking pillar also called Eros Tower / Vega North Tower, a 5,280 ft sub-summit north of Morning Star's main summit). Route-finding landmarks: pass just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees, thread a natural gap through the trees into a second open talus field, cross open heather and more talus, cross a strip of trees near a rocky bluff, then ascend to the obvious red gully to the right of the buttress. A convenient seep just below the Mile High gully is the only reliable water on the approach, and only runs through mid-season. From the gully, scramble up and left on rubble-strewn, loose ledges (careful footing/rockfall management for parties below) to a lone fir tree, then follow a narrow ledge about 20 ft to a single bolted belay marking the start of Pitch 1. Plan roughly 1–1.5 hours from the trailhead to the base once you know the line; it is unmarked past the switchback and has caught out parties who don't have beta or GPS coordinates for the turnoff.

text: Descend by rappelling the route itself, back down the same line you climbed — do not try to walk off. Eight single-strand rappels, all off bolted, fixed anchors (this is a sport-bolted line, so no natural gear or v-threads needed): rap 1 from the P7/summit anchor down to the anchor at the base of pitch 7; rap 2 face-rappels to an anchor set left and above the dihedral; rap 3 is a short drop to a ledge-side anchor beside the dihedral; rap 4 goes to one of two anchors at the pitch 4 stance (favor the left one); rap 5 is a short, free-hanging rap off an upper-P3 anchor aimed at a ~10 ft tree left of the line, with an intermediate anchor in a nook below it; rap 6 is a vertical face rappel down lower P3 to a large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors; rap 7 drops to the pitch 1 anchor (10–15 ft left of the original belay); rap 8 finishes at the base. A single 70m rope is sufficient for all 8 raps; two 60m ropes also work if you'd rather split gear or prefer doubled-rope security, and some parties carry a single 60m instead but report tighter/more numerous transitions. Because you rappel the entire route back to the start, many parties leave approach shoes and packs stashed at the base. Descent hazards: loose rock sitting on several of the belay ledges (manage ropes and stack carefully to avoid kicking debris onto the party below), some rope-stretch/rope-snag potential given the zigzagging (not straight-down) line of anchors, and lingering steep snow in the approach gully in spring that can complicate the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.

text: Start at the Sunrise Mine trailhead at the end of the forest road. The first mile crosses two unbridged creeks — a log, a root crossing and one more insistent ford — so expect wet feet and treat them seriously in early-season high water. The trail then climbs steadily through forest to the last major switchback before it starts zigzagging steeply up toward the pass. That switchback is where you leave the trail; the pass is not. From there a cairned line traverses northeast across talus. Route-finding markers on the traverse, in order: pass just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees, thread a natural gap through those trees into a second open talus field, cross heather and more talus, cross a strip of trees near a rocky bluff. A seep just below the gully is the only reliable water and only runs mid-season.

text: The traverse ends at the obvious red gully on the right-hand side of the buttress. From the gully, scramble up and left on rubble-strewn ledges to a lone fir tree, then follow a narrow ledge about twenty feet to a single bolted belay — one bolt, on a ledge, past one tree. That belay is the start of the first pitch and there is nothing else like it on this tower. Negative markers: if you are standing on open talus under a dark grey face with two large boulders at its foot and a long line of bolts running away up a fifty-five-metre pitch, you are one line left of here, on the west-face route that shares this tower's summit; if you left the traverse into a gully on the right-hand (east) side of the tower and climbed cedar and heather to a notch on the skyline, you are on the neighbouring tower entirely and the route above you is a different climb.

text: Mix-up Peak (7,440 ft) sits one mile south of Cascade Pass on the Skagit–Chelan county line and marks the northern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse. First climbed in 1947 by Wesley Grande and Jack Kendrick, its East Face is a compact, mostly solid-rock 'staircase' of class 3–4 scrambling with a short mid-5th-class step near the top, reached by a glacier/snowfield crossing from Cascade Pass. It's a popular objective (7-9 hours from the trailhead to the summit alone) for parties already in the Cascade Pass basin, but the approach's moat and rockfall-prone notches keep it a genuine alpine outing despite the modest elevation.

text: Descend by reversing the final scramble pitches/downclimbing back to the top of the technical face (the uppermost section is a downclimb/scramble to the top of the East Face), then begin a rappel sequence rather than trying to downclimb the buttress itself — the rock is loose enough that down-climbing the route is not recommended. From a small ledge/anchor on the east side just below the summit, a 50 m rappel gets you down the steepest upper wall (rockfall-prone — the next rappeller should move off to the side immediately, not straight down, to avoid anyone above). Below that, from the bottom of the shoulder, one rappel on a single 60 m rope reaches the belay station at the top of the second climbing pitch. From there the line drops over an overhanging section to just below the north side of Gunsight Notch: one double-rope rappel with two ropes, or two rappels on a single 60 m rope. That is four rappels on one 60 m rope, which is what parties report, or three with two ropes. Anchors are fixed natural slings and cord rather than bolts, and parties regularly add cord or rebuild one, so carry some. Move off the fall line as soon as you are down each rappel; rockfall knocked loose by the party above is a recognized hazard here. Below the notch, re-descend the glacier and snowfield and Mixup Arm to Cascade Pass.

text:
There are two notches at the head of the Cache Glacier on Mixup's east side, and picking the wrong one is the standard mistake.

A U-shaped notch sits on the left and a V-shaped notch on the right. The East Face is accessed from the V-notch. It is common — and accepted — to go up through the U-notch on the left and wrap around the back side to reach the V, so being at the U is not a failure, but starting to climb from it is.

Gunsight Notch, the prominent notch west of Cache Col, is the portal that serves Mix-Up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak, and the snow tongue leading to it is short, about a hundred feet, but steep at roughly 50-65 degrees. Bergschrunds flank the tongue on either side, dropping ten to fifteen feet to a rock floor, and the ground between the snow and the rock is wet, tight and swept by rockfall.

From the south side of the notch the sequence is specific and is your confirmation: go west about 100 ft down a side gully, then ascend northwest up a wide, loose gully to a saddle. At that saddle the White Staircase begins — an easy, exposed class 3 staircase of pale grey rock on the right-hand side of the large summit pyramid. If you are looking at a grey staircase-like ramp on the right side of the pyramid, you are exactly where you should be.

The hardest and dirtiest climbing on the whole approach is the first fifty feet out of the moat where the glacier meets rock — perhaps mid-fifth on loose ground. That difficulty is itself a tell: if the entry felt trivial, check that you have actually crossed the moat at the right place.

Season matters for this specifically. As the Cache Glacier recedes, getting to the notch has been getting harder year on year, and by August the moat can be the deciding problem rather than the climbing.

text: Monument Peak is the most rugged and inaccessible peak in the Lago group, deep in the eastern Pasayten Wilderness near the Eureka Creek country. Double-nubbed and built of granite, it sits almost as an island: Eureka Creek wraps its north, west, and south sides while Monument Creek drains the east side. The mountain has a precipitous north/northeast side, a cliffy east face, a rugged west face, and a comparatively gentler (though still remote) south slope that forms the standard scramble line. A disheveled connecting ridge links it to 8,397-ft Blackcap Mountain a half-mile north; 8,745-ft Mount Lago, its line parent, lies about 2.4 miles further north. First ascended in 1978 by Fred Beckey and John Roper.

text: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FR-4065 off the Mountain Loop Highway), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (Trail #707) about half a mile. Just before the trail crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish River, leave it for a faint abandoned path on the river's east side, or take the line of least resistance along that side. The path soon fades into slide alder, brush and rock debris; fording the river to dodge the brush is hazardous in high runoff, especially in late spring and early summer. Work up the valley past a house-sized boulder near 3,100 ft, then either cross the river and climb a ridge ramp southwest to the upper basin (about 4,000 ft), or continue to a broad basin at about 3,700 ft and climb the steep gully (or the slabs to its right) directly east of it, leaving it to the right where that is easy. Climb snow-covered slabs to a notch in Morning Star's southeast ridge at about 5,600 ft; these slabs are the route's main avalanche concern. The round trip is roughly 5.5-6 miles with 3,700-4,200 ft of gain. The steep gully is often icy when snow-filled, so helmet, ice axe and crampons are standard early in the season; early-season snow makes this a basic alpine climb rather than a scramble.

text: From the Killen Creek Trailhead (FS Rd 2329, ~3 miles from Takhlakh Lake), follow Killen Creek Trail #113 through open, dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles in you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows (last reliable easy water before the high basin), then the trees thin as the trail climbs rockier terrain to meet the PCT (Trail #2000) at roughly 6,100 ft, about 3.1 miles from the trailhead. Continue straight across the PCT onto the High Camp Trail #10 for about 1.0 mile to High Camp / Adams Glacier Meadows at the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine (~6,900 ft) — a common base camp. From High Camp the route leaves maintained trail: traverse east/southeast, off-trail across lava fields and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, crossing the toe of the Lava Glacier, to reach the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This traverse is glacier/talus travel with real route-finding, especially in low-snow years — a rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on glacier ice. The Lyman Glacier itself splits around a rock outcrop; the north lobe (original route) and south lobe (40° lower half on unbroken neve/ice, upper half broken by crevasses and serac walls) both lead to a crux chute near 10,000 ft that varies 45–65° for about 50 ft depending on the year, then easier snow to the summit plateau.

text:
From the Killen Creek trailhead, follow Trail #113 through open dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows — the last easy water before the high basin. The trees thin as the trail climbs rockier ground to the PCT at about 6,100 ft, roughly 3.1 miles in. Continue straight across onto High Camp Trail #10 for about a mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, near 6,900 ft.

From High Camp the maintained trail is done. Traverse east and southeast off-trail across lava fields, across the toe of the Lava Glacier and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, to the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This is glacier and talus travel with real route-finding, worst in a low-snow year; rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on ice.

Most of the route can be simul-climbed with a running belay on pickets. The standard descent is the North Ridge, not a reversal — long, loose volcanic scree, occasionally narrow, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below.

edits.new: over lava fields and across the toe of the Lava Glacier, then around or across the toe of Lava Ridge, to the foot of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft

text:
Count the ridges, and for this route you must get past two.

East of High Camp the order is: Adams Glacier, North Ridge, Lava Glacier, Lava Ridge, Lyman Glacier. You cross the Lava Glacier and then go around or over the toe of Lava Ridge. Lava Ridge is the second ridge and it is the gate. If you have crossed only one ridge and stopped at a glacier, you are at the Lava Glacier Headwall — a different climb with a triangular face — not at the Lyman.

The positive test is a fork, and it is unmistakable once you are on it: the Lyman splits around a narrow rock outcrop into two lobes. The north lobe is the original line; the south lobe runs 40-degree unbroken neve on its lower half and is broken by crevasses and serac walls on its upper half. A glacier that forks around an island of rock is the confirmation you are where you meant to be.

The crux confirms it a second time, higher: both lobes lead to a chute near 10,000 ft that runs anywhere from 45 to 65 degrees over about 50 ft depending on the year. One short steep chute, then easier snow to the summit plateau. If you meet no constriction at all, you are on a neighbouring glacier.

The base elevation is the third check: about 8,000 ft. Arriving on ice much higher than that means you gained the glacier well above its toe and may have come onto it over the ridge rather than around it, which is fine but changes where the lobes sit relative to you.

What the descent means for the approach, and it is worth deciding at the car: you do not come back this way. The walk-off is the North Ridge, back toward High Camp. So the ridge you counted past on the way in is not the ridge you come down.

edits.old: go around or over the toe of Lava Ridge
edits.new: pass around or across the toe of Lava Ridge

text: An easy glacier climb with long stretches of steep glacier travel and an optional short technical pitch at the very top. From Sunrise Camp, ascend a 40° glacier, then veer right up a 45° headwall to a narrowing strip of glacier leading to Piker's Peak; climbers may exit left on a 25-30° field or continue right through an optional 60-70° snow/ice section.

From about 10,000 ft snowfields lead on, including one steep section with no runout above the Lava Glacier, to the ice cap near 12,000 ft; then walk about a mile across the summit plateau to the summit.

text: A Mt. Adams Climbing Pass is required from 1 May to 30 September for anyone 16 or older going above 7,000 ft, whether or not they intend to summit; it is bought on Recreation.gov and must be carried on you and shown in the vehicle windscreen. From October through April a self-issued wilderness permit replaces it. Human waste must be packed out in carry-out bags (free at the Mt. Adams Ranger District) because decomposition above 7,000 ft is too slow to keep up. Group size limit is 12; no campfires.

text: Drive Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) to its end at the Austin Pass/Artist Point trailhead, a paved lot roughly 58 miles and 1.5-2 hours from Bellingham. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and overnight parties sign the wilderness register at the trailhead; no camping permit is needed. The upper highway to Austin Pass typically doesn't open until late June or early July, depending on snowpack, and the trailhead has had weekend-focused access in recent seasons, so check current alerts before planning a start time.

text:
From the Austin Pass / Artist Point trailhead at the end of SR-542, follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600. It drops about 800 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up to a saddle at 4,900 ft northwest of Lake Ann, about 3.9 miles one way; the lake itself is a short way farther down the trail.

From the saddle, leave the maintained trail for a boot path heading southwest then south along the ridge crest. Where the ridge steepens near 5,300 ft the path contours the east side before the crest re-forms; from there follow cairns over Peak 5681 and scramble roughly half a mile west along the summit ridge to Mount Ann.

About 10.5 miles round trip with roughly 4,000 ft of cumulative gain, part of which comes from the fact that the trail loses 800 ft at the start and you pay it back at the end.

Note on the name: this is the Lake Ann below Artist Point on SR-542, not the Lake Ann near Maple Pass. One route has already been recorded with the wrong Lake Ann's trailhead.

text: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs are not allowed at Easy Pass or anywhere beyond it, because the national park begins at the pass.

text: Cockscomb Ridge is the true north ridge of Mount Baker — a long, prominent rock-and-ice ridge forming a skyline on the north side of the peak, distinct from the popular 'North Ridge' route (which is actually the NW spur). It sits between the North Ridge and the Park Glacier Headwall and is approached from the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead across the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers. First climbed in its entirety on July 4, 1961 by Chuck Murley, John Musser, and a third climber, after a 1906 Mazama party had been turned back by the ridge's 300-ft Cockscomb Tower.

text: A sustained Grade IV ice route up the broken Coleman Glacier's northwest headwall, and one of the more technically complex routes regularly climbed on Baker. From a high camp near 6,600-7,000 ft, the route crosses the broken lower Coleman Glacier to the base of the headwall around 8,500 ft, then climbs roughly 10-14 pitches of sustained 45-50 degree snow/ice with several short steeper steps (occasionally 60-80 degrees) and a crux bergschrund passage near 10,000 ft before easing onto the summit plateau. Most parties start well before dawn and take 8-12 hours camp-to-summit.
